14:T2fba,<p>I wrote <a href="/v2/rust-ate-javascript-build-toolchain">a whole post</a>, a history of JavaScript build tools being replaced by Rust one after another: SWC replacing Babel, Turbopack replacing Webpack. That post keeps saying Rust is faster. Faster by how much?</p>
<p>So let's run some benchmarks, all on the same machine.</p>
<h2>Seven scenarios, from Node 16% faster to Rust 35x faster</h2>
<p>At most, Rust is about 35 times faster than Node.</p>
<iframe src="/embeds/rust-bench-spectrum" width="100%" height="450" loading="lazy" style="border:0;overflow:hidden;max-width:700px;display:block;margin:1.5rem auto;" title="Rust against Node, seven scenarios"></iframe>
<p>Adding up ten million floating point numbers: Node 9.78ms, Rust 9.65ms, nearly identical. Every step waits for the previous addition (s = s + this number), one floating point addition takes about 3 cycles, and both sides run at that speed. Changing the language does not help.</p>
<p>Allocating lots of small objects that are thrown away right after use, Node is actually faster: a median of 4.34ms per round against Rust's 5.05ms. V8's generational GC is built for exactly this. New objects go into one contiguous block of memory (the young generation), so allocating is just moving a pointer forward; when the block is full, the program stops, the few objects still alive are moved, and the rest of the block is cleared at once. In Rust, each object asks the allocator for its own memory and is freed one by one.</p>
<p>But in the rounds where GC stops the program, Node gets slower. In the slowest 1% (p99), Node is 10.34ms and Rust 5.74ms. In one run with <code>--trace-gc</code>, GC stopped 275 times over the 200 rounds, the longest stop 4.29ms.</p>
<p>The 35x at the right end is "multiply each number by two and add it up if it passes a threshold", written as <code>map().filter()</code>. Node's <code>map</code> builds an array of ten million items, <code>filter</code> builds another, and the whole chain takes 578ms; the same work as a hand written for loop takes 62ms. A Rust iterator builds no intermediate array: each number is doubled, checked against the threshold and added in one pass, and it compiles to the same thing as the hand written loop, 16.1ms.</p>
<h2>Small arrays: Node is faster. Large arrays: Rust is faster</h2>
<p>Same code, only the array length changes.</p>
<iframe src="/embeds/rust-bench-dataflip" width="100%" height="430" loading="lazy" style="border:0;overflow:hidden;max-width:620px;display:block;margin:1.5rem auto;" title="One branch: Node faster on small arrays, Rust faster on large ones"></iframe>
<figure data-rehype-pretty-code-figure=""><pre tabindex="0" data-language="python" data-theme="github-dark github-light"><code data-language="python" data-theme="github-dark github-light" style="display: grid;"><span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">for</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> each number </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">in</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> the array:</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">    y </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">=</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> number </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">*</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5"> 2</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">    if</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> y </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">></span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5"> 1</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">:  total </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">=</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> total </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">+</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> y    </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D"># add it</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">    else</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">:      total </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">=</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> total        </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D"># skip, unchanged</span></span></code></pre></figure>
<p>The data is random, so the <code>if</code> is true about half the time. The total work is fixed at reading two hundred million elements, so a shorter array is walked more times; the chart shows <strong>the time per element</strong>.</p>
<p>As the array grows, Node slows down and Rust does not, because the two compile that <code>if</code> into different machine code.</p>
<p><strong>Node keeps the branch.</strong> The CPU does not wait for the comparison; it guesses a path from which way this branch went the last few times and keeps running. This is branch prediction. A right guess costs nothing; a wrong guess throws away what was computed on that path and starts over. In the chart, as the array grows from a thousand to a million items, Node goes from 1.02ns to 5.59ns per element. Another run uses an array of ten million items and changes the condition to one that is almost always true, so the CPU always guesses right: Node drops from 6.26ns to 3.64ns per element, while Rust stays at about 1.57ns both times.</p>
<p><strong>Rust has no branch.</strong> LLVM computes both results, with and without the addition, and picks one with <code>fcsel</code>, a select instruction. Each element costs one extra addition, but the CPU has nothing to guess.</p>
<p>Here are the inner loops both sides actually compile to, written as assembly, one CPU instruction per line:</p>
<figure data-rehype-pretty-code-figure=""><pre tabindex="0" data-language="asm" data-theme="github-dark github-light"><code data-language="asm" data-theme="github-dark github-light" style="display: grid;"><span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">; Rust: no jump, fcsel picks one of two</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">ldr   d1, [x10], #</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">8</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">      ; load one number</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">fadd</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">  d1, d1, d1         </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">; y = number * 2</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">fadd</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">  d2, d0, d1         </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">; compute total + y first</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">fcmp  d1, d12            </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">; compare y with 1.0</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">fcsel d0, d2, d0, gt     </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">; y > 1: take total + y, otherwise keep total</span></span></code></pre></figure>
<figure data-rehype-pretty-code-figure=""><pre tabindex="0" data-language="asm" data-theme="github-dark github-light"><code data-language="asm" data-theme="github-dark github-light" style="display: grid;"><span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">; Node (V8's TurboFan): b.hs jumps over the add</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">ldr   d0, [x4, x6]       </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">; load one number</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">fadd</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">  d0, d0, d0         </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">; y = number * 2</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">fcmp  d1, d0             </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">; compare 1.0 with y</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">b.hs  #+</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">0x8</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">              ; y not above 1: skip the next line</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">fadd</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">  d2, d2, d0         </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">; total = total + y</span></span></code></pre></figure>
<p>With a short array, the sequence of "add / skip" keeps repeating and fits within what the branch predictor records, so it guesses right almost every time. Once the array is too long for that, about half the guesses are wrong. On this M1 Pro the boundary falls between four thousand and sixteen thousand elements. Rust has no branch to guess, so at any length each element takes about 1.58ns, the flat line in the chart.</p>
<h2>SWC claims 20 to 70x. How much of that is Rust?</h2>
<p>SWC claims to be <a href="https://swc.rs/">20 times faster than Babel on one thread and 70 times faster on four cores</a>.</p>
<p>The test closest to a bundler builds an AST (abstract syntax tree) of 1.78 million nodes and walks it: Node 39.62ms, Rust 14.79ms, a gap of 2.68x. That is how much the language alone accounts for; 20 divided by 2.7 leaves about 7x to explain.</p>
<p>esbuild, written in Go, is the comparison: like SWC it is a native binary designed from scratch, only the language is not Rust.</p>
<iframe src="/embeds/rust-bench-esbuild" width="100%" height="310" loading="lazy" style="border:0;overflow:hidden;max-width:620px;display:block;margin:1.5rem auto;" title="Compile time: Babel vs SWC vs esbuild"></iframe>
<p>Compiling the same 280KB file to ES2019: Babel 134ms, SWC 19.6ms, esbuild 25.6ms. Each tool ran six times, and esbuild was 20 to 30% slower than SWC every time, but both were more than five times faster than Babel. That 5x is not something only Rust has.</p>
<p>Compiling to ES5: Babel 4385ms, SWC 78.1ms, a gap of 56x. esbuild does not support ES5.</p>
<p>Dividing SWC's two multiples over Babel, 6.8x for ES2019 and 56x for ES5, by the language's 2.7x leaves 2.5x for ES2019 and 21x for ES5. That remainder comes from Babel and SWC being written differently.</p>
<p>The four cores in the 70x are not all Rust's doing either. Running the same work on eight threads, Node gets 6.2 times faster and Rust 7.6 times. Rust gains a bit more, but Node still gets six times faster with its built in worker threads splitting the work across cores; Babel simply does not use them.</p>
<h2>What SWC's multiple is made of</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>About 3x, the language</strong>: moving from JavaScript to a language that compiles to a native binary. The AST walk is 2.7x; for a job that runs once and exits, such as reading a 4.8MB file, rewriting it and writing it back, it is 2.7 to 3.7x including startup, and most of the extra is Node's startup: <code>node -e 0</code>, which does nothing, still takes 34.8ms.</li>
<li><strong>2.5 to 21x, how the program is written</strong>: this part grows with the work. Switching the target from ES2019 to ES5 makes Babel's time 33 times longer and SWC's only 4 times.</li>
<li><strong>About 3.5x, multiple cores</strong> (SWC's own 70 divided by 20): Node has worker threads too; Babel does not use them.</li>
</ul>
<p>Only the first part has to do with the language, and esbuild, written in Go, has that part too.</p>
<p>The toolchain post is <a href="/v2/rust-ate-javascript-build-toolchain">here</a>.</p>15:T1d12,
I wrote [a whole post](/v2/rust-ate-javascript-build-toolchain), a history of JavaScript build tools being replaced by Rust one after another: SWC replacing Babel, Turbopack replacing Webpack. That post keeps saying Rust is faster. Faster by how much?

So let's run some benchmarks, all on the same machine.

## Seven scenarios, from Node 16% faster to Rust 35x faster

At most, Rust is about 35 times faster than Node.

<iframe src="/embeds/rust-bench-spectrum" width="100%" height="450" loading="lazy" style="border:0;overflow:hidden;max-width:700px;display:block;margin:1.5rem auto;" title="Rust against Node, seven scenarios"></iframe>

Adding up ten million floating point numbers: Node 9.78ms, Rust 9.65ms, nearly identical. Every step waits for the previous addition (s = s + this number), one floating point addition takes about 3 cycles, and both sides run at that speed. Changing the language does not help.

Allocating lots of small objects that are thrown away right after use, Node is actually faster: a median of 4.34ms per round against Rust's 5.05ms. V8's generational GC is built for exactly this. New objects go into one contiguous block of memory (the young generation), so allocating is just moving a pointer forward; when the block is full, the program stops, the few objects still alive are moved, and the rest of the block is cleared at once. In Rust, each object asks the allocator for its own memory and is freed one by one.

But in the rounds where GC stops the program, Node gets slower. In the slowest 1% (p99), Node is 10.34ms and Rust 5.74ms. In one run with `--trace-gc`, GC stopped 275 times over the 200 rounds, the longest stop 4.29ms.

The 35x at the right end is "multiply each number by two and add it up if it passes a threshold", written as `map().filter()`. Node's `map` builds an array of ten million items, `filter` builds another, and the whole chain takes 578ms; the same work as a hand written for loop takes 62ms. A Rust iterator builds no intermediate array: each number is doubled, checked against the threshold and added in one pass, and it compiles to the same thing as the hand written loop, 16.1ms.

## Small arrays: Node is faster. Large arrays: Rust is faster

Same code, only the array length changes.

<iframe src="/embeds/rust-bench-dataflip" width="100%" height="430" loading="lazy" style="border:0;overflow:hidden;max-width:620px;display:block;margin:1.5rem auto;" title="One branch: Node faster on small arrays, Rust faster on large ones"></iframe>

```python
for each number in the array:
    y = number * 2
    if y > 1:  total = total + y    # add it
    else:      total = total        # skip, unchanged
```

The data is random, so the `if` is true about half the time. The total work is fixed at reading two hundred million elements, so a shorter array is walked more times; the chart shows **the time per element**.

As the array grows, Node slows down and Rust does not, because the two compile that `if` into different machine code.

**Node keeps the branch.** The CPU does not wait for the comparison; it guesses a path from which way this branch went the last few times and keeps running. This is branch prediction. A right guess costs nothing; a wrong guess throws away what was computed on that path and starts over. In the chart, as the array grows from a thousand to a million items, Node goes from 1.02ns to 5.59ns per element. Another run uses an array of ten million items and changes the condition to one that is almost always true, so the CPU always guesses right: Node drops from 6.26ns to 3.64ns per element, while Rust stays at about 1.57ns both times.

**Rust has no branch.** LLVM computes both results, with and without the addition, and picks one with `fcsel`, a select instruction. Each element costs one extra addition, but the CPU has nothing to guess.

Here are the inner loops both sides actually compile to, written as assembly, one CPU instruction per line:

```asm
; Rust: no jump, fcsel picks one of two
ldr   d1, [x10], #8      ; load one number
fadd  d1, d1, d1         ; y = number * 2
fadd  d2, d0, d1         ; compute total + y first
fcmp  d1, d12            ; compare y with 1.0
fcsel d0, d2, d0, gt     ; y > 1: take total + y, otherwise keep total
```

```asm
; Node (V8's TurboFan): b.hs jumps over the add
ldr   d0, [x4, x6]       ; load one number
fadd  d0, d0, d0         ; y = number * 2
fcmp  d1, d0             ; compare 1.0 with y
b.hs  #+0x8              ; y not above 1: skip the next line
fadd  d2, d2, d0         ; total = total + y
```

With a short array, the sequence of "add / skip" keeps repeating and fits within what the branch predictor records, so it guesses right almost every time. Once the array is too long for that, about half the guesses are wrong. On this M1 Pro the boundary falls between four thousand and sixteen thousand elements. Rust has no branch to guess, so at any length each element takes about 1.58ns, the flat line in the chart.

## SWC claims 20 to 70x. How much of that is Rust?

SWC claims to be [20 times faster than Babel on one thread and 70 times faster on four cores](https://swc.rs/).

The test closest to a bundler builds an AST (abstract syntax tree) of 1.78 million nodes and walks it: Node 39.62ms, Rust 14.79ms, a gap of 2.68x. That is how much the language alone accounts for; 20 divided by 2.7 leaves about 7x to explain.

esbuild, written in Go, is the comparison: like SWC it is a native binary designed from scratch, only the language is not Rust.

<iframe src="/embeds/rust-bench-esbuild" width="100%" height="310" loading="lazy" style="border:0;overflow:hidden;max-width:620px;display:block;margin:1.5rem auto;" title="Compile time: Babel vs SWC vs esbuild"></iframe>

Compiling the same 280KB file to ES2019: Babel 134ms, SWC 19.6ms, esbuild 25.6ms. Each tool ran six times, and esbuild was 20 to 30% slower than SWC every time, but both were more than five times faster than Babel. That 5x is not something only Rust has.

Compiling to ES5: Babel 4385ms, SWC 78.1ms, a gap of 56x. esbuild does not support ES5.

Dividing SWC's two multiples over Babel, 6.8x for ES2019 and 56x for ES5, by the language's 2.7x leaves 2.5x for ES2019 and 21x for ES5. That remainder comes from Babel and SWC being written differently.

The four cores in the 70x are not all Rust's doing either. Running the same work on eight threads, Node gets 6.2 times faster and Rust 7.6 times. Rust gains a bit more, but Node still gets six times faster with its built in worker threads splitting the work across cores; Babel simply does not use them.

## What SWC's multiple is made of

- **About 3x, the language**: moving from JavaScript to a language that compiles to a native binary. The AST walk is 2.7x; for a job that runs once and exits, such as reading a 4.8MB file, rewriting it and writing it back, it is 2.7 to 3.7x including startup, and most of the extra is Node's startup: `node -e 0`, which does nothing, still takes 34.8ms.
- **2.5 to 21x, how the program is written**: this part grows with the work. Switching the target from ES2019 to ES5 makes Babel's time 33 times longer and SWC's only 4 times.
- **About 3.5x, multiple cores** (SWC's own 70 divided by 20): Node has worker threads too; Babel does not use them.

Only the first part has to do with the language, and esbuild, written in Go, has that part too.

The toolchain post is [here](/v2/rust-ate-javascript-build-toolchain).
16:T2948,:T2bad,<p>我寫過<a href="/v2/rust-ate-javascript-build-toolchain">一整篇</a>，JavaScript build 工具被 Rust 一個一個換掉的血淚史，SWC 換掉 Babel，Turbopack 換掉 Webpack。那篇一直說 Rust 比較快，到底快多少？</p>
<p>就來跑跑看 benchmark 吧，都在同個環境。</p>
<h2>七種情境，從 Node 快 16% 到 Rust 快 35 倍</h2>
<p>Rust 對 Node 最多差到 35 倍左右。</p>
<iframe src="/embeds/rust-bench-spectrum" width="100%" height="450" loading="lazy" style="border:0;overflow:hidden;max-width:700px;display:block;margin:1.5rem auto;" title="Rust 對 Node 的速度，七種情境"></iframe>
<p>一千萬個浮點數相加，Node 9.78ms、Rust 9.65ms，幾乎一樣。每一步都要等上一步加完（s = s + 這一筆），一次浮點加法大約 3 個 cycle，兩邊都停在這個速度，換語言也沒用。</p>
<p>大量配置用完就丟的小物件，Node 反而比較快，每一輪的中位數是 4.34ms，Rust 是 5.05ms。V8 的 generational GC 就是為這種情況設計的：新物件都放進一塊連續的記憶體（young generation），配置只要把指標往後移；放滿了就停下來，把少數還活著的搬走，剩下的整塊清掉。Rust 則是每個物件各自向 allocator 要記憶體，用完再一個一個還回去。</p>
<p>不過碰到 GC 停下來的那幾輪，Node 就變慢了。最慢的 1%（p99）Node 是 10.34ms，Rust 是 5.74ms。用 <code>--trace-gc</code> 跑一次，200 輪裡 GC 一共停了 275 次，最長的一次 4.29ms。</p>
<p>最右邊那個 35 倍，是把「每個數字乘二、過門檻就加總」寫成 <code>map().filter()</code>。Node 的 <code>map</code> 先產生一個一千萬筆的陣列，<code>filter</code> 再產生一個，整段要 578ms；同樣的事用手寫 for 迴圈只要 62ms。Rust 的 iterator 不產生中間陣列，每個數字從乘二、比門檻到加總一次做完，編譯出來跟手寫迴圈一樣，16.1ms。</p>
<h2>小陣列 Node 快，大陣列 Rust 快</h2>
<p>同一段 code，只改陣列長度。</p>
<iframe src="/embeds/rust-bench-dataflip" width="100%" height="430" loading="lazy" style="border:0;overflow:hidden;max-width:620px;display:block;margin:1.5rem auto;" title="同一個判斷，小陣列 Node 快、大陣列 Rust 快"></iframe>
<figure data-rehype-pretty-code-figure=""><pre tabindex="0" data-language="python" data-theme="github-dark github-light"><code data-language="python" data-theme="github-dark github-light" style="display: grid;"><span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">掃過陣列裡每個數字:</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">    y </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">=</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> 數字 </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">*</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5"> 2</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">    如果 y </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">></span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5"> 1</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">:  total </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">=</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> total </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">+</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> y    </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D"># 加進去</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">    否則:        total </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">=</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> total        </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D"># 跳過,不變</span></span></code></pre></figure>
<p>資料是亂數，所以那個 <code>if</code> 大約一半成立。總工作量固定在讀兩億個元素，陣列越短就重複走越多遍，圖上畫的是<strong>每個元素花的時間</strong>。</p>
<p>陣列一長，Node 就變慢，Rust 不會，原因是兩邊把那個 <code>if</code> 編譯成不一樣的 machine code。</p>
<p><strong>Node 留著分支。</strong> CPU 不等比較結果出來，先照這個分支最近幾次的走向猜一條路往下跑，這叫 branch prediction。猜對沒有成本，猜錯就把那條路上算好的丟掉重來。圖上陣列從一千筆拉長到一百萬筆，Node 每個元素從 1.02ns 升到 5.59ns。另一組用一千萬筆的陣列，把條件換成幾乎永遠成立，讓 CPU 每次都猜對，Node 每個元素就從 6.26ns 降到 3.64ns，而 Rust 前後都是 1.57ns 左右。</p>
<p><strong>Rust 沒有分支。</strong> LLVM 把加了跟沒加的結果都先算好，再用 <code>fcsel</code> 這條二選一的指令挑一個。每個元素多算一次加法，但 CPU 沒有東西要猜。</p>
<p>下面是兩邊實際編譯出來的內迴圈，寫成 assembly，一行就是一條 CPU 指令：</p>
<figure data-rehype-pretty-code-figure=""><pre tabindex="0" data-language="asm" data-theme="github-dark github-light"><code data-language="asm" data-theme="github-dark github-light" style="display: grid;"><span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">; Rust：沒有跳躍，用 fcsel 二選一</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">ldr   d1, [x10], #</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">8</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">      ; 讀一個數字</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">fadd</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">  d1, d1, d1         </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">; y = 數字 * 2</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">fadd</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">  d2, d0, d1         </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">; total + y 先算好</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">fcmp  d1, d12            </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">; y 跟 1.0 比</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">fcsel d0, d2, d0, gt     </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">; y > 1 就取 total + y，否則留原本的 total</span></span></code></pre></figure>
<figure data-rehype-pretty-code-figure=""><pre tabindex="0" data-language="asm" data-theme="github-dark github-light"><code data-language="asm" data-theme="github-dark github-light" style="display: grid;"><span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">; Node（V8 的 TurboFan）：b.hs 會跳過加法</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">ldr   d0, [x4, x6]       </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">; 讀一個數字</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">fadd</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">  d0, d0, d0         </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">; y = 數字 * 2</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">fcmp  d1, d0             </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">; 1.0 跟 y 比</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">b.hs  #+</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">0x8</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">              ; y 不大於 1 就跳過下一行</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">fadd</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">  d2, d2, d0         </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">; total = total + y</span></span></code></pre></figure>
<p>陣列短的時候，那串「加／跳」一直重複，整串都在 branch predictor 的記錄範圍內，幾乎都猜對。陣列長到超出範圍，就有一半猜錯。這台 M1 Pro 的分界在四千到一萬六千筆之間。Rust 沒有分支要猜，不管陣列多長，每個元素都是 1.58ns 左右，就是圖上那條平線。</p>
<h2>SWC 說的 20 到 70 倍，有多少是 Rust 的功勞</h2>
<p>SWC 宣稱<a href="https://swc.rs/">單執行緒比 Babel 快 20 倍、四核心快 70 倍</a>。</p>
<p>最接近 bundler 的那組，是建一棵 178 萬個節點的 AST（abstract syntax tree）再走訪一遍，Node 39.62ms、Rust 14.79ms，差 2.68 倍。語言本身就差這麼多，20 倍除以 2.7，還有大約 7 倍要另外找原因。</p>
<p>拿 Go 寫的 esbuild 來對照，它跟 SWC 一樣是原生執行檔、從頭設計，只是語言不是 Rust。</p>
<iframe src="/embeds/rust-bench-esbuild" width="100%" height="310" loading="lazy" style="border:0;overflow:hidden;max-width:620px;display:block;margin:1.5rem auto;" title="Babel 對 SWC 對 esbuild 的編譯時間"></iframe>
<p>同一個 280KB 的檔案編譯成 ES2019，Babel 134ms，SWC 19.6ms，esbuild 25.6ms。每個工具各跑六次，esbuild 每次都比 SWC 慢兩到三成，但兩個都比 Babel 快五倍以上，這五倍不是 Rust 才有。</p>
<p>編譯成 ES5 的話，Babel 4385ms，SWC 78.1ms，差 56 倍。esbuild 不支援 ES5。</p>
<p>SWC 比 Babel 快的這兩個倍數，ES2019 的 6.8 倍跟 ES5 的 56 倍，各自除以語言的 2.7 倍，ES2019 還剩 2.5 倍，ES5 還剩 21 倍。剩下的這些倍數，是 Babel 跟 SWC 兩個程式寫法不同造成的。</p>
<p>70 倍裡的四核心，也不全是 Rust 的功勞。同一份工作開八個執行緒，Node 快 6.2 倍，Rust 快 7.6 倍。Rust 多拿了一點，但 Node 也快了六倍，用內建的 worker threads 就能把工作分給每個核心，Babel 只是沒用而已。</p>
<h2>SWC 的倍數是怎麼組成的</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>大約 3 倍，語言</strong>：從 JavaScript 換成編譯成原生執行檔的語言。AST 走訪是 2.7 倍；跑一次就結束的工作，例如讀一個 4.8MB 的檔、改寫後寫回，算上啟動是 2.7 到 3.7 倍，多出來的大多是 Node 的啟動時間，<code>node -e 0</code> 什麼都不做也要 34.8ms。</li>
<li><strong>2.5 到 21 倍，程式寫法</strong>：工作越重，這部分越大。目標從 ES2019 換成 ES5，Babel 的時間變成 33 倍，SWC 只變成 4 倍。</li>
<li><strong>大約 3.5 倍，多核心</strong>（SWC 自己的 70 除以 20）：Node 也有 worker threads，Babel 沒用。</li>
</ul>
<p>只有第一項跟語言有關，而 Go 寫的 esbuild 也有這一項。</p>
